content.p: In May 1980, the city of Gwangju, the capital of South Jeolla province in the southwest of South Korea, rose against a military government. For ten days, students and then ordinary residents fought paratroopers in the streets, took control of much of the city and held it for a short time before the army returned in force. The revolt was crushed on 27 May. Four decades later it is still one of the most contested episodes in South Korean history, both for the number of people killed and for who gave the orders that killed them.

The uprising grew out of the political vacuum left when President Park Chung-hee was assassinated on 26 October 1979 by his intelligence chief, Kim Jae-gyu, according to the Korea Herald. Hopes rose for a democratic opening. Instead, Maj. Gen. Chun Doo-hwan, who headed the Defense Security Command, seized control of the military in a coup on 12 December 1979, according to the Korea Times and the Japan Times.

Students kept demonstrating through the spring of 1980. On 17 May, Chun's junta extended martial law across the whole country, closed universities, banned political activity and tightened controls on the press. In the early hours of 18 May, Kim Dae-jung, the opposition politician from the same province, and 25 other opposition leaders were arrested, according to the Gwangju News chronology.

On 18 May, paratroopers from the 7th Airborne Brigade took up positions at Chonnam National University and Chosun University. Students who came to the campus gates were turned away and went out onto the streets instead. Gwangju News says the 33rd and 35th Battalions of the 7th Airborne Brigade were deployed overnight into 18 May to the two campuses, taking control of both universities.

Gwangju News records that residents set fire to two police stations on 19 May, and that a student of the Chosun University affiliated high school was the first wounded by troops' gunfire that day. The Truth Commission later placed the first shot in front of Gwangju High School at about 4:50 p.m. on 19 May.

By 20 May, the army had cut the city's landline connections, so news of what was happening did not reach the rest of the country. The Korea Herald's own coverage was shaped by the same censorship; its 23 May issue called the events a "bloody riot" and reported that nine people had been confirmed dead. The newspaper's 2023 retrospective says that over 50 protesters were killed in a standoff on 21 May, including a pregnant woman, and that its 23 May 1980 edition did not report this.

On the evening of 20 May, drivers of taxis, buses and trucks gathered at Mudeung Stadium and drove a convoy down Geumnam-ro, the main road, carrying protesters toward the provincial office. Gwangju News says the convoy was stopped by police and troops after a standoff, and that a bus charge at a police line that night killed four officers. Later that night, troops fired on unarmed people at the Gwangju Station plaza, according to the same chronology.
content.h2: The citizen militia and the Provincial Office
content.p: The violence changed the protest. Asia Times says that after the killings non-student townspeople joined the uprising, which forced a temporary military retreat to the outskirts of the city. The Nation credits the armed resistance of Gwangju's citizen militia with liberating the city, and describes the self-organised period that followed, which it calls the Gwangju Commune, when townspeople kept the city running, buried their dead and ran mutual aid.

Asia Times, in a 2016 account by a reporter who entered the city on 26 May 1980 for the Baltimore Sun, describes the militia's spokesman, Yun Sang-won, who asked the reporter to convey a request for American mediation to the US ambassador. The reporter says the spokesman refused to give his name at the time, and said the group would "fight to the last man". Asia Times reports that fellow fighters later told the reporter that Yun had been shot in the kidney area when he came out of his office with a weapon, and that a grenade set fire to the curtain he had been wrapped in. These details come from survivors and family members as the reporter recorded them in 1993, not from an official record.

Troops re-entered the city early on 27 May. Asia Times says the spokesman and several holdouts were shot, and that Yun was found dead among ashes. The Nation says that within days of the White House meeting on 22 May, which its reporters first described in 1996, the US commander in Korea released two divisions of Korean troops from the joint command.

No single figure for the dead has been accepted by all sides, and the official numbers have changed with each review. In 1980, the official count was about 200, according to the Associated Press and VOA, while the South China Morning Post reports that more than 200 were dead or missing. The Korea Times put the toll at 193, including 166 civilians, and counted 376 more deaths in the aftermath, which it said were a direct consequence of the events. Japan Times calls the official figure of 170 discredited.

The Truth Commission, which began work in 2020 after a 2018 law was introduced to reopen the probe, reported in May 2023, reconstructed the troops' movements and produced a narrower account. It concluded that troops fired more than fifty shots at people in more than twenty places across Gwangju and South Jeolla in May 1980, and that 135 of the dead had died of gunshot wounds, according to Kyunghyang Shinmun. A defence ministry record listed 166 civilians dead, and the commission said more than 80 per cent of them were shot. Among the dead, it counted eight minors aged fourteen or younger and twelve women.

Injuries were counted separately. The commission counted 2,617 people hurt, using hospital and compensation files. Of the 442 people injured on 18 May, 44 later had disabilities of grade 9 or higher. The commission said many victims still carried bullets 43 years later. The Korea Times reported an official tally of around 160 killed and 1,000 injured, and said people in Gwangju believed the true numbers were two to three times that figure. The two sets of figures are not reconciled, and each source says who produced its figure.

Residents, families and activists have long said that more people died than the records show. Gwangju News reports that the May 18 Bereaved Families Association counted seventy-six civilians still missing, presumed dead. The Truth Commission has exhumed remains in places including Yeongam, near Haenam, and the hills in front of the Gwangju Prison.
content.h2: Helicopters, orders and the question of who gave them
content.p: The commission's most contested finding concerns who ordered the troops to fire. It said that more than seventy military witnesses in the chain of command pointed to Chun Doo-hwan, then head of the Defense Security Command, as the man behind the shooting, and that it would name whoever was responsible. A former assistant director of human resources at Army Headquarters told Kyunghyang Shinmun that the order to fire was not given in writing. The Korea Times reports that Chun has said he did not order soldiers to open fire.

Helicopters are the second disputed point. A defence ministry committee reported in 2018 that the army had fired from helicopters on civilians on 21 and 27 May, and called the attacks premeditated. It could not find who ordered them, because helicopter operation logs had not been kept or could not be found. The Korea Times reported that former officers under Chun had said there were no such attacks. The 2023 commission found a 20mm bullet at Chosun University that it linked to a Cobra helicopter, which it said was the first time a bullet had been confirmed, 34 years after a former regional commander told the National Assembly the helicopter had fired there.

The Korea Times reports Chun's denials in detail. He testified in the National Assembly in December 1989 and denied responsibility. His 2017 memoir described the uprising as a riot, and he called a Catholic priest who testified about helicopter shootings a liar. Chun was on trial for defamation over those remarks when he died. The Korea Times records that he never apologised.
content.h2: The United States and the trials
content.p: The role of the United States is a separate and contested question. The Nation, whose reporters first described a White House meeting on 22 May 1980 in 1996, writes that Carter's national security team gave the green light for troops to retake the city, and offered Chun short-term backing if he accepted long-term political change. Its reporters say the notes of a senior Pentagon official show that the White House knew by then that 60 people had been shot to death in Gwangju and over 400 injured. The Nation adds that Washington has repeatedly framed Gwangju as South Korea's own internal affair. VOA reports that US officials say they lacked influence and adequate real-time information, and that US ambassadors visit Gwangju but do not issue formal apologies.

After the uprising, Kim Dae-jung was arrested and sentenced to death by a military tribunal for allegedly fomenting it. The AP says that after the US intervened, his sentence was reduced and he was later freed. Chun, meanwhile, went on to become president. According to Asia Times, the government put out two versions: one blamed Kim Dae-jung, and the other blamed North Korean agents. The Asia Times reporter says he reported solid evidence that the government had invented the North Korean theory and spread it as disinformation.

Chun was tried after democracy returned. Under President Kim Young-sam, both men were tried. The court found them guilty of mutiny and treason, with the coup and the crackdown in Gwangju at the centre of the charges, and of corruption. Chun received a death sentence and Roh was given 22 and a half years. The Supreme Court reduced the sentences, and NBC reports that Chun's became life imprisonment and Roh's 17 years. NBC reports that both men got out in late 1997, freed by a special pardon that President-elect Kim Dae-jung had asked for, with national unity as the aim. The AP says Kim Young-sam, the president, granted the pardon at that request.

Chun was also ordered to return 220 billion won, about $185 million, in the bribery case, according to Korea Times. The AP puts the sum at $190 million. Chun said he had only 290,000 won in his bank account, and more than 90 billion won remained uncollected when he died.

An apology from the state came slowly. In 2018 the defence minister, Jeong Kyeong-doo, apologised for rapes and sexual torture committed by martial law troops, after a protester said on television that she had been raped by an interrogator in 1980. The SCMP reports that the investigation confirmed 17 cases, and that victims included teenagers and a pregnant woman who was not taking part in the protests.

Ahead of the 40th anniversary in 2020, President Moon Jae-in promised full support for a new, independent fact-finding committee, according to VOA. The Truth Commission delivered its final report in May 2023. By then, Chun had died in November 2021, aged 90. His widow, Lee Soon-ja, apologised for the "pains and scars" caused during her husband's time in office, without naming any misdeed, NBC reports. A senior official at a foundation representing Gwangju victims called the apology vague and said it rang hollow, NBC reports.

The uprising remains a symbol. The BBC quotes the Korean novelist and former dissident Hwang Sok-yong saying that the Kwangju Uprising "lit the fuse of the dynamite stick of democracy". Public anger at Chun's rule fed mass protests in 1987, and NBC reports that Chun then accepted a constitutional change to allow a direct vote for president, which is considered the start of South Korea's transition to democracy. The investigation into the massacre, one victims' group says, is not over.
